title: Slow performance with encryption on an Intel Xeon E5-2407
body: I am running Proxmox 8.0 (Debian 12), kernel 6.2.16-10-pve, and OpenZFS 2.1.12-pve1 on an Intel Xeon E5-2407. My encrypted pool uses three mirrored VDEVs with SATA SSDs and AES-256-GCM. A sequential fio read test with 4K blocks reaches only 66 MB/s with ZFS encryption versus about 400 MB/s without it. The CPU supports AES-NI and AVX, and aesni_intel is loaded. I can reproduce this by creating an encrypted pool on a Sandy Bridge-era Xeon and benchmarking it. There are no useful log messages.

symptoms_visible: My 4K sequential fio read test reaches about 66 MB/s with AES-256-GCM ZFS encryption, compared with about 400 MB/s without ZFS encryption on this Xeon E5-2407 system.
N0.label: N0 encrypted-read slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: The large-block OpenSSL AES-256-GCM benchmark reaches about 760 MB/s, while the ZFS encrypted read remains much slower.
The affected pool uses mirrored VDEVs rather than RAIDZ, and this CPU has AVX but not AVX2.
N1.label: N1 independent crypto and configuration evidence collected

symptoms_visible: With a 10 GiB file and 4K reads, the encrypted pool delivers about 40.9 MB/s while the unencrypted pool delivers about 595 MB/s.
Repeated tests on the encrypted pool range around 400–650 MB/s when the file is cached but only 30–40 MB/s when reading from disk.
N2.label: N2 larger-file 4K comparison recorded

symptoms_visible: With recordsize and fio block size both set to 1 MiB and compression disabled, the unencrypted dataset reaches about 895 MB/s but the encrypted dataset reaches only about 47.3 MB/s.
Average reported latency is about 22.15 ms with ZFS encryption versus about 1.16 ms without it.
N3.label: N3 recordsize-aligned benchmark confirms slowdown

symptoms_visible: On the same machine, an Ext4 filesystem inside a LUKS2 loop device reaches about 274 MB/s with the same 1 MiB fio read workload, while the ZFS-encrypted dataset reaches about 47 MB/s.
N4.label: N4 alternative encryption performs substantially faster

symptoms_visible: On Debian 12 with kernel 6.2.16, the icp parameters list GCM implementations as 'cycle [fastest] generic pclmulqdq'; AVX is absent from that list even though the CPU supports AVX.
N5.label: N5 current-kernel ICP implementation output collected

symptoms_visible: I corrected my comparison: on the same E5-2407, Debian 11 with kernel 5.15.108 and ZFS 2.1.11 lists 'cycle [fastest] avx generic pclmulqdq', while Debian 12 with kernel 6.2.16 and ZFS 2.1.12 does not list AVX.
N6.label: N6 cross-kernel ICP regression established

symptoms_visible: My last posted comparison still shows AVX available to the ZFS GCM implementation on the older kernel but absent on the affected newer kernel; I did not post a performance retest after the patched kernels became available.
N_terminal.label: terminal kernel fix reported without reporter retest

question_patterns: Can you run an OpenSSL AES-256-GCM speed test on this CPU and paste the raw results?
What throughput does an independent AES-256-GCM benchmark report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With `openssl speed -evp aes-256-gcm`, I get about 735–761 MB/s at 1 KiB through 16 KiB block sizes; OpenSSL is 3.0.9.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: OpenSSL AES-256-GCM also tops out near 45 MB/s at large block sizes.
OpenSSL reaches about 700 MB/s rather than 760 MB/s at large block sizes.

question_patterns: Do you have any cryptsetup benchmark results from the same machine?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. `cryptsetup benchmark` reports AES-XTS at about 989 MB/s for a 256-bit key and about 794 MB/s for a 512-bit key.

question_patterns: How much RAM does the machine have, and what is the ARC size?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have 32 GB of RAM. ARC is currently around 7 GB and can grow to 16 GB.

edges.comment: Issue comments c1-c4, reporter's system only: the reporter volunteered independent crypto throughput, clarified that the pool uses mirrors and the CPU has AVX but no AVX2, and answered the RAM/ARC question.

question_patterns: Can you repeat the fio comparison with a file larger than the initially tested 1 GiB and paste both raw results?
Please compare encrypted and unencrypted reads using a 10 GiB test file so cache effects are more visible.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With a 10 GiB file and the default 4 KiB fio block size, I get 40.9 MB/s on the encrypted 3x2 SSD pool and 595 MB/s on the unencrypted 2x1 SSD mirror.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both encrypted and unencrypted 10 GiB tests run at roughly 550 MB/s.
The encrypted run is 45 MB/s and the unencrypted run is 560 MB/s.

question_patterns: Does fio print any warning about the selected I/O engine and queue depth?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. fio says that synchronous I/O and iodepth are both selected, so the queue depth is capped at one.

edges.comment: Issue comments c5-c7, reporter's system: after cache behavior was questioned, the reporter ran and pasted 10 GiB 4K tests. These are measurement results, not a diagnosis.

question_patterns: Can you set recordsize to 1 MiB, use a 1 MiB fio block size, disable compression, and compare encrypted with unencrypted reads?
Please rerun with matching 1 MiB recordsize and block size to measure maximum sequential throughput.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With recordsize=1M, `--bs=1M`, and compression disabled, the unencrypted dataset reaches 895 MB/s. An encrypted dataset in the same mirror pool reaches 47.3 MB/s.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: At 1 MiB recordsize and block size, encrypted throughput rises to about 800 MB/s and nearly matches the unencrypted result.
The same test reports 50 MB/s encrypted and 850 MB/s unencrypted.

question_patterns: What average latency does fio report for each of those 1 MiB runs?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The encrypted run reports average latency of 22152.62 microseconds; the unencrypted run reports 1160.15 microseconds.

edges.comment: Issue comments c8-c13, reporter's system: maintainers requested a block size aligned with recordsize, and the reporter pasted both 1 MiB results. The raw throughput and latency establish that 4K syscall overhead does not explain the gap.

question_patterns: Can you run the same fio workload through another encryption implementation, such as a LUKS partition, on this machine?
Please compare against LUKS or gocryptfs to determine whether other disk encryption is similarly slow.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I created a 20 GB file on the unencrypted mirror, used it as a loop device with Ext4 on LUKS2 using aes-xts-plain64, and ran the same 1 MiB test. Even with those layers, it reaches about 274 MB/s.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The LUKS2 test also runs at only about 45 MB/s.
The LUKS2 test reaches about 250 MB/s instead of 274 MB/s.

edges.comment: Issue comments c13-c15, reporter's system: a participant requested an alternative-encryption fio test, and the reporter returned the raw LUKS2 result. The conclusion that hardware alone is not the bottleneck is engineer-side reasoning.

question_patterns: Please run `grep . /sys/module/icp/parameters/icp_*` on the affected system and paste the exact output.
Which AES and GCM implementations are listed by the loaded icp module?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On Debian 12 with kernel 6.2.16, I get `icp_aes_impl:cycle [fastest] generic x86_64 aesni`, `icp_gcm_avx_chunk_size:32736`, and `icp_gcm_impl:cycle [fastest] generic pclmulqdq`. I initially thought Debian 11 gave the same result.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The affected Debian 12 system lists `avx` as the fastest GCM implementation.
The implementation order differs, but AVX is still absent from the Debian 12 GCM list.

edges.comment: Issue comments c16-c18, reporter's system: participant1 requested the icp parameter output. The reporter pasted raw output and initially stated that Debian 11 behaved the same; no kernel-root-cause conclusion is placed in the user's answer.

question_patterns: Can you double-check the icp output from the older Debian 11 environment on the same CPU?
Please paste the exact older-kernel GCM implementation line so we can compare it with Debian 12.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Correction: on the same E5-2407, Debian 11 with kernel 5.15.108 and ZFS 2.1.11 reports `icp_gcm_impl:cycle [fastest] avx generic pclmulqdq`. Debian 12 with kernel 6.2.16 and ZFS 2.1.12 reports `cycle [fastest] generic pclmulqdq` without AVX.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: After checking again, both kernels list AVX identically.
The older kernel lists AVX in a different order, but it is present there and absent on the newer kernel.

edges.comment: Issue comment c19, reporter's system: the reporter voluntarily corrected the earlier Debian 11 claim and supplied the exact cross-kernel output. The correction is retained as a separate knowledge step so the earlier mistaken report is not silently rewritten.

solution.intent: Treat the slowdown as a Linux kernel regression affecting X86_FEATURE_OSXSAVE and therefore ZFS's availability of the AVX GCM implementation; update to a kernel containing the corresponding fix, then rerun the encrypted benchmark before declaring the performance issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Install a patched Proxmox or distribution kernel that includes the OSXSAVE regression correction. Confirm that the icp GCM implementation list again includes AVX, then rerun the same encrypted 1 MiB fio test. A Proxmox maintainer reported the correction was queued for the next 6.2 kernel and had already fixed the regression in testing, but the original reporter did not post a retest.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied only benchmark results and the differing raw icp implementation lists. Maintainers later identified the final accepted cause as a Linux kernel regression involving X86_FEATURE_OSXSAVE and reported that the kernel correction restored the expected behavior. Mapping the missing AVX entry to that kernel regression is engineer inference, not something the reporter independently diagnosed.

edges.comment: Issue comments c18-c24: participant1 connected the missing AVX implementation to kernel FPU behavior; participant4 reported that a patched Proxmox kernel had fixed the regression in internal testing; participant5 later identified the final accepted cause as the Linux X86_FEATURE_OSXSAVE regression. No affected reporter posted a patched-kernel retest, so the terminal state records a shipped/reported fix without user-perceived resolution.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as a Linux kernel regression involving X86_FEATURE_OSXSAVE, which prevented the AVX GCM implementation from being available to ZFS on the affected newer kernel.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: strong independent crypto throughput, the large encrypted-versus-unencrypted ZFS gap, substantially faster LUKS performance, and AVX appearing in the older kernel's icp GCM list but not the affected newer kernel's list.
Must not dismiss the result as merely an inherently slow Sandy Bridge CPU or as only a 4K fio/syscall artifact; the alternative-encryption and recordsize-aligned tests contradict those explanations.
Must recommend using a kernel containing the OSXSAVE regression correction rather than changing pool topology or replacing the CPU as the primary fix.

Must ask the reporter to verify the icp implementation output and encrypted fio performance on a patched build before declaring the issue resolved; the thread contains maintainer confirmation but no reporter retest.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Linux and storage administrator who can create ZFS datasets, LUKS loop devices, change recordsize, run fio and crypto benchmarks, inspect kernel module parameters, and compare operating-system environments, but relies on maintainers to interpret kernel and ZFS implementation details.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative and evidence-driven; pastes detailed command output, follows requested benchmark changes, clarifies hardware and pool topology, and explicitly corrects earlier statements when a comparison was mistaken.
